text: Vincent Joseph Schaefer (July 4, 1906 – July 25, 1993) was an American chemist and meteorologist who developed cloud seeding. On November 13, 1946, while working at the General Electric Research Laboratory, he seeded clouds in the Berkshire Mountains using dry ice. Self-taught and never having completed high school, Schaefer held 14 patents. He was the oldest son of Peter Aloysius Schaefer and Rose Agnes (Holtslag) Schaefer, and had two younger brothers, Paul and Carl, and two younger sisters, Gertrude and Margaret. The family resided in Schenectady, New York, and due to his mother's health, began summer trips to the Adirondack Mountains in 1921. Schaefer maintained a lifelong connection with the Adirondacks and had interests in hiking, natural history, and archaeology. In his youth, he founded a local group of the Lone Scouts and co-wrote and printed a publication called "Archaeological Research," which introduced him to key figures in Schenectady, including Dr. Willis Rodney Whitney of the General Electric Research Laboratory. During the late 1920s and early 1930s, he built a personal library on natural history and science and organized several groups, including the Mohawk Valley Hiking Club (1929), the Van Epps-Hartley Chapter of the New York Archaeological Association (1931), and the Schenectady Wintersport Club (1933–34), which established snow trains to ski slopes in the Adirondacks. In 1931, he began work on creating the Long Path of New York, a hiking trail from near New York City to Whiteface Mountain. He also developed adult education programs on natural history, expanding his community connections, including with John S. Apperson, a GE engineer and conservationist, who introduced him to Irving Langmuir, a Nobel Prize-winning scientist at GE Research Laboratory known for surface chemistry. Langmuir shared Schaefer’s passion for skiing and outdoor activities. During his retirement, Schaefer collaborated with photographer John Day on *A Field Guide to the Atmosphere* (1981), a Peterson Field Guide publication. He devoted time to environmental issues, natural and local history, writing numerous articles and giving presentations on upstate New York’s natural environment and human impact. He actively supported the preservation of wilderness areas and parks such as the Mohonk Preserve, Vroman's Nose, and the Great Flats Aquifer. His interest in Dutch barns led him to edit *Dutch Barn Miscellany* and build a scale model of one. He conducted research on original settler families in Schenectady and the Mohawk Valley. In retirement, he prepared timelines, an unpublished autobiography, indexes to his research notebooks and film collections, and arranged the disposition of his papers and library. He also worked on a project titled "Ancient Windows of the Earth," involving thin slicing of rocks to create translucent, stained-glass-like effects that revealed geologic history. As part of this, he designed and built a 6-foot-diameter window in memory of his parents for Saint James Church in North Creek, the Adirondacks. Schaefer married Lois Perret on July 27, 1935, and lived on Schermerhorn Road in Schenectady in a house built with his brothers, which they called Woestyne South; Woestyne North was the name of their Adirondack camp. They had three children: Susan, Katherine, and James. In 1922, his parents asked him to leave high school to work, and with advice from his maternal uncles, he enrolled in a four-year apprentice machinist course at General Electric. During his second year, he took a one-month leave to join Dr. Arthur C. Parker on an archaeological expedition in central New York. After completing the apprenticeship in 1926, he worked at the GE Research Laboratory machine shop as a journeyman toolmaker. Disappointed by this work, he joined the Davey Institute of Tree Surgery in 1927 through correspondence, worked briefly in Michigan, and then returned to Schenectady as an independent landscape gardener. With Robert Palmer’s advice in 1929, he declined a partnership in a plant nursery and rejoined the machine shop as a model maker. At the machine shop, he built equipment for Langmuir and his research associate, Katharine B. Blodgett. In 1932, Langmuir appointed Schaefer as his research assistant, and in 1933, Schaefer began working with Langmuir, Blodgett, Whitney, and others at the Research Laboratory and throughout GE. Together, they published reports on surface chemistry techniques, electron microscopy, polarization, ice surface affinity, protein monolayers, protein films, television tube brightness, and submicroscopic particulates. A lasting contribution was the 1938 description of the Langmuir–Schaefer method, a technique for the controlled transfer of a monolayer to a substrate, a modification of the Langmuir–Blodgett method. After being promoted to research associate in 1938, Schaefer continued working with Langmuir on national advisory committee projects, especially related to military matters before and during the Second World War, including research on gas mask filtration, submarine detection using binaural sound, and artificial fog generation via smoke generators, which was demonstrated at Vrooman's Nose in the Schoharie Valley for military observers. During his time as Langmuir’s assistant, Schaefer was allowed to pursue his own research, such as in 1940, when he developed a method to create replicas of individual snowflakes using a thin plastic coating, which brought him national attention and widespread correspondence from individuals, including students. In 1943, Schaefer and Langmuir shifted focus to precipitation static, aircraft icing, ice nuclei, and cloud physics, conducting many experiments at Mount Washington Observatory in New Hampshire. In the summer of 1946, Schaefer found his "cold box" too warm for needed tests and, determined to proceed, placed dry ice into its bottom. By breathing into the box and observing a sudden bluish haze that transformed into millions of microscopic ice crystals under strobe light, he discovered that a sudden change in temperature and humidity in supercooled water spontaneously produced billions of ice nuclei. Through repeated experiments, he developed a method to "seed" supercooled clouds with dry ice. In November 1946, Schaefer successfully seeded a natural cloud by airplane, producing a dramatic ice and snow effect. The publicity led to numerous requests from individuals and businesses for snow and water, as well as from scientists worldwide working on weather modification. The discovery sparked debates about altering nature through cloud seeding. The successful field test enabled Langmuir to secure federal funding for further cloud seeding and weather modification research at the GE Research Laboratory. Schaefer served as coordinator of the laboratory portion of Project Cirrus, while the Air Force and Navy provided aircraft and pilots for field tests and data collection. Field tests were conducted in the Schenectady area, Puerto Rico, and New Mexico. When military pilots were reassigned during the Korean War, GE recommended discontinuing Project Cirrus after comprehensive reports were prepared; the final report was issued in March 1953. While Project Cirrus was ending, Schaefer was approached by Vernon Crudge on behalf of the Munitalp Foundation to work on its meteorological research program. For a time, he worked for both the Research Laboratory and Munitalp, and in 1954 left the Research Laboratory to become Director of Research at Munitalp. At Munitalp, he collaborated with the U.S. Forest Service at the Priest River Experimental Forest in northern Idaho with Harry T. Gisborne, a noted fire researcher, on Project Skyfire, which aimed to determine how cloud seeding could influence lightning patterns in thunderstorms and reduce forest fires. Project Skyfire originated from a connection between the Forest Service and Schaefer established during early Project Cirrus days. While at Munitalp, he also developed a mobile atmospheric research laboratory and produced time-lapse films of clouds. He left Munitalp in 1958, declining an offer to move to Kenya with the Foundation, but remained an adviser for several years afterward. After leaving Munitalp, Schaefer focused on scientific education, promoting hands-on experimentation over book learning. He worked with the American Meteorological Society and the Natural Science Foundation on an educational film program and helped establish the Natural Sciences Institute (NSI) summer programs, allowing high school students to conduct field research and experiments with scientists. From 1959 to 1961, he served as director of the Atmospheric Science Center at the Loomis School in Connecticut. In the 1970s, he organized and led annual winter expeditions for 8–10 research scientists to Yellowstone National Park, where geysers like Old Faithful produced large amounts of supercooled clouds at temperatures between negative 20 and negative 50 Fahrenheit. Researchers used dry ice and silver iodide to convert supercooled water to ice crystals at ground level, enabling direct observation of halo and corona optical effects. From 1962 to 1968, the NSI program continued under Schaefer’s directorship under the Atmospheric Sciences Research Center (ASRC) at the State University of New York at Albany. During this time, he also maintained consulting work with companies, government agencies, and universities throughout his career, extending beyond his retirement from ASRC in 1976. Schaefer helped found ASRC in 1960 and served as its Director of Research until 1966, when he became Director. He recruited qualified atmospheric science researchers to ASRC, many of whom had worked on Project Cirrus, including Bernard Vonnegut, Raymond Falconer, and Duncan Blanchard. During his tenure at ASRC, in addition to the NSI summer programs, he led annual research expeditions to Yellowstone each January. In the 1970s, his research interests shifted to solar energy, aerosols, gases, air quality, and atmospheric pollution particles. His work culminated in a three-part report on Air Quality on the Global Scale in 1978. During the 1970s, he also taught in the American Association for the Advancement of Science Chautauqua short courses for science teachers. The work spans 405 pages and includes 15 chapters, illustrations, and black-and-white photographs.
